At it's simplest, you can measure time by tracking the progress of physical events such as the sun and moon progressing through the sky in regular patterns. This, on its own, is evidence for the existence of time, at least in the sense of a progression of physical events, or observable change. Evidence for this is all around us, given that understanding.

But at a deeper level, space (dimensionality) is relativistically inseparable from time, and vice versa, which we now call spacetime.

Analyzing an understanding of time that is dependent on dimensionality results in stunning and interesting results, not the least of which is that time slows or speeds relative to the distance of a gravity source (known as time dilation). And if you rewind the universe back to the point of the Big Bang Singularity (BBS), you discover that the BBS is a zero-point entity, meaning that we encounter a definite thing that has no dimensions, is therefore also timeless, and is uncaused, as nothing could exist as a precursor. That would, by definition, suggest a time before the timeless.

A little evidence? Quentin Smith summarizes:

(Source: Quentin Smith, Philosophy of Science, 1988; The Uncaused Beginning of the Universe) There is sufficient evidence at present to justify the belief that the universe began to exist without being caused to do so. This evidence includes the Hawking-Penrose singularity theorems that are based on Einstein's General Theory of Relativity, and the recently introduced Quantum Cosmological Models of the early universe. The singularity theorems lead to an explication of the beginning of the universe that involves the notion of a Big Bang singularity, and the Quantum Cosmological Models represent the beginning largely in terms of the notion of a vacuum fluctuation. Theories that represent the universe as infinitely old or as caused to begin are shown to be at odds with or at least unsupported by these and other current cosmological notions.

(Note also the ESA's Planck space telescope which demonstrated "an almost perfect fit to the standard model of cosmology" that materializes from the BBS.)

The BBS is also the most chaotic and unpredictable thing imaginable, leading Stephen Hawking to correct Einstein's insistence for a deterministic universe, by saying, "God not only plays dice. He sometimes throws them where they can't be seen." That is to say, not even God could predict what would come out of the Big Bang Singularity. It's literally unknowable.

(Source) By combining space and time into a single manifold called Minkowski space, physicists have significantly simplified a large number of physical theories, as well as described in a more uniform way the workings of the universe at both the supergalactic and subatomic levels.
